Given that ${\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r=16,$ evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=xy\,i+y\,j$ and $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the fact that

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r.
$$

We're given the value of the first integral, so we only need to work out the second.

The path ${C}_{2}$ is the section of the curve $y=-{x}^{3}$ from $A$ to $O.$ It can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}(t)=t\,i-{t}^{3}\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $-2\le t\le 0.$ Along this curve, we have $x=t$ and $y=-{t}^{3}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{2}(t)) & =xy\,i+y\,j \\  & =-{t}^{4}\,i-{t}^{3}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivative, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-{t}^{3})j \\  & =i-3{t}^{2}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

We can now compute the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{2}(t))\cdot {r}_{2}^{′}(t) & =(-{t}^{4}\,i-{t}^{3}\,j)\cdot (i-3{t}^{2}\,j) \\  & =-{t}^{4}+3{t}^{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =16+{\int }_{-2}^{0}F({r}_{2}(t))\cdot {r}_{2}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =16+{\int }_{-2}^{0}(-{t}^{4}+3{t}^{5})\,\text{d}t \\  & =16+{[-\frac{1}{5}{t}^{5}+\frac{1}{2}{t}^{6}]}_{-2}^{0} \\  & =16+[0-(-\frac{(-{2}^{5})}{5}+\frac{(-2)^{6}}{2})] \\  & =16-\frac{192}{5} \\  & =-\frac{112}{5}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b523b1e1-5cbd-5efb-b1af-a137b9b5cd25"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-b523b1e1-5cbd-5efb-b1af-a137b9b5cd25" :answer-field/id #uuid "b523b1e1-5cbd-5efb-b1af-a137b9b5cd25" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-7527daea-f713-54e2-9b27-ffd3fc3bb110" :answer-field/choices ["answer-7527daea-f713-54e2-9b27-ffd3fc3bb110" "answer-e3cf1e9e-5de9-575b-be80-c45bb969b3f6" "answer-55fc80b9-6193-508c-b227-e04b2840c9d6" "answer-e0ded463-bc16-568f-8c0b-62a6554bc47d" "answer-ff980988-6413-52f6-84a6-6d1daa6d7016"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7527daea-f713-54e2-9b27-ffd3fc3bb110" :answer/id #uuid "7527daea-f713-54e2-9b27-ffd3fc3bb110" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{112}{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e3cf1e9e-5de9-575b-be80-c45bb969b3f6" :answer/id #uuid "e3cf1e9e-5de9-575b-be80-c45bb969b3f6" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{23}{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-55fc80b9-6193-508c-b227-e04b2840c9d6" :answer/id #uuid "55fc80b9-6193-508c-b227-e04b2840c9d6" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{51}{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e0ded463-bc16-568f-8c0b-62a6554bc47d" :answer/id #uuid "e0ded463-bc16-568f-8c0b-62a6554bc47d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{32}{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ff980988-6413-52f6-84a6-6d1daa6d7016" :answer/id #uuid "ff980988-6413-52f6-84a6-6d1daa6d7016" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{8}{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-3412530f-81b3-51bb-95a9-4599a55eb207" :question/id #uuid "3412530f-81b3-51bb-95a9-4599a55eb207" :question/math-academy-id "q-77250" :question/problem "![](images/87/87182d625f4e669a6b2791a17f3e12c34922043b8f3deefd6b2473e8fb529886.png)

Consider a vector field $\mathbf F$ on $\mathbb R^2$ with components $P$ and $Q\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\mathbf F(x,y) = P(x,y)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y)\,\mathbf j
$$

Now suppose that $C$ is a smooth curve on $\mathbb R^2,$ given by

$$
\mathbf r (t) = x(t)\,\mathbf i + y(t)\,\mathbf j, \qquad t\in [a,b].
$$

Then, we can write the line integral of $\mathbf F$ along $C$ as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}(P(x(t),y(t))\,i+Q(x(t),y(t))\,j)\cdot (\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j)\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}(P(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+Q(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}P(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+Q(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{C}P(x,y)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following formula:

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F\cdot\textrm d \mathbf r  = \int\limits_C P(x,y)\,\textrm d x + Q(x,y)  \,\textrm d y
$$

An analogous result holds for vector fields on $\mathbb R^3.$ That is, 

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F\cdot\textrm d \mathbf r  = \int\limits_C P(x,y,z)\,\textrm d x + Q(x,y,z)  \,\textrm d y + R(x,y,z) \,\textrm d z
$$

where $\mathbf F(x,y,z) = P(x,y,z)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y,z)\,\mathbf j + R(x,y,z)\,\mathbf k.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186180678 :tutorial/content "Since there is a fundamental link between line integrals of vector-valued functions and line integrals with respect to $x$ and $y,$ it should be unsurprising that they share similar properties. We list two of them below:

- If $-C$ denotes the path obtained by reversing the orientation of $C,$ then

$$
\int\limits_{-C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r = -\int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r.
$$

- If $C = C_1\cup C_2$ is the union of two paths $C_1$ and $C_2$, then

$$
\int\limits_{C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r 
= 
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r + \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r.
$$

The first property has an intuitive meaning if we think about it in terms of the work done by a force on a particle. To see this, consider the vector field $\mathbf F$ and the line segment $\overline{AB},$ shown below. Let $C$ be the path defined by traversing the line segment from $A$ to $B.$

![](images/4f/4f69f80d98d301410908f7ec867a89bdc834c22a51f224d9b00b80ceca39ab87.png)

 

Let $W(C)$ be the work done in moving the particle along $C.$ Since our particle moves in the same direction as the vector field, we have

$$
W(C) = \int\limits_{C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r > 0.
$$

However, if we move the particle from $B$ to $A,$ we expect the line integral to be negative. This is because the particle is now moving against $\mathbf F.$ 

![](images/fe/fe6b2e67d33a4993104406c88b1dc0dc897be33d034007ed581a75f741ddf620.png)

 

Therefore,

$$
W(-C) = \int\limits_{-C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r < 0.
$$

We can show that the work done in moving the particle along $-C$ is the same as the work done in moving it along $C$ but with the opposite sign. That is

$$
W(-C) = -W(C).
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\int\limits_{-C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r = -\int\limits_{C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186179857 :activity/expected-seconds 660.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

The path ${C}_{2}$ is the section of the curve $y=-{x}^{3}$ from $A$ to $O.$ It can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}(t)=t\,i-{t}^{3}\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $-2\le t\le 0.$ Along this curve, we have $x=t$ and $y=-{t}^{3}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{2}(t)) & =xy\,i+y\,j \\  & =-{t}^{4}\,i-{t}^{3}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-{t}^{3})j \\  & =i-3{t}^{2}\,j\end{aligned}

$$

Consider a vector field $\mathbf F$ on $\mathbb R^2$ with components $P$ and $Q\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\mathbf F(x,y) = P(x,y)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y)\,\mathbf j
$$

Now suppose that $C$ is a smooth curve on $\mathbb R^2,$ given by

$$
\mathbf r (t) = x(t)\,\mathbf i + y(t)\,\mathbf j, \qquad t\in [a,b].
$$

Then, we can write the line integral of $\mathbf F$ along $C$ as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}(P(x(t),y(t))\,i+Q(x(t),y(t))\,j)\cdot (\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j)\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}(P(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+Q(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}P(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+Q(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{C}P(x,y)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following formula:

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F\cdot\textrm d \mathbf r  = \int\limits_C P(x,y)\,\textrm d x + Q(x,y)  \,\textrm d y
$$

An analogous result holds for vector fields on $\mathbb R^3.$ That is, 

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F\cdot\textrm d \mathbf r  = \int\limits_C P(x,y,z)\,\textrm d x + Q(x,y,z)  \,\textrm d y + R(x,y,z) \,\textrm d z
$$

where $\mathbf F(x,y,z) = P(x,y,z)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y,z)\,\mathbf j + R(x,y,z)\,\mathbf k.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186180678 :tutorial/content "Since there is a fundamental link between line integrals of vector-valued functions and line integrals with respect to $x$ and $y,$ it should be unsurprising that they share similar properties. We list two of them below:

- If $-C$ denotes the path obtained by reversing the orientation of $C,$ then

$$
\int\limits_{-C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r = -\int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r.
$$

- If $C = C_1\cup C_2$ is the union of two paths $C_1$ and $C_2$, then

$$
\int\limits_{C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r 
= 
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r + \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r.
$$

The first property has an intuitive meaning if we think about it in terms of the work done by a force on a particle. To see this, consider the vector field $\mathbf F$ and the line segment $\overline{AB},$ shown below. Let $C$ be the path defined by traversing the line segment from $A$ to $B.$

![](images/4f/4f69f80d98d301410908f7ec867a89bdc834c22a51f224d9b00b80ceca39ab87.png)

 

Let $W(C)$ be the work done in moving the particle along $C.$ Since our particle moves in the same direction as the vector field, we have

$$
W(C) = \int\limits_{C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r > 0.
$$

However, if we move the particle from $B$ to $A,$ we expect the line integral to be negative. This is because the particle is now moving against $\mathbf F.$ 

![](images/fe/fe6b2e67d33a4993104406c88b1dc0dc897be33d034007ed581a75f741ddf620.png)

 

Therefore,

$$
W(-C) = \int\limits_{-C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r < 0.
$$

We can show that the work done in moving the particle along $-C$ is the same as the work done in moving it along $C$ but with the opposite sign. That is

$$
W(-C) = -W(C).
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\int\limits_{-C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r = -\int\limits_{C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186179857 :activity/expected-seconds 660.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}] "assertions" [["question-a47f5f1d-1328-52e8-8c90-bfca32946e28" :question/id #uuid "a47f5f1d-1328-52e8-8c90-bfca32946e28"] ["question-a47f5f1d-1328-52e8-8c90-bfca32946e28" :question/math-academy-id "q-125419"] ["question-a47f5f1d-1328-52e8-8c90-bfca32946e28" :question/problem "Let $F(x,y)={e}^{y}\,i+{e}^{x}\,j$ and let $C$ be the path defined by $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2},\,t-1⟩$ for $t\in [0,1].$ Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r?$"] ["question-a47f5f1d-1328-52e8-8c90-bfca32946e28" :question/worked-solution "Given a piecewise-smooth path $C$ and a vector field

Given that ${\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r=16,$ evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=xy\,i+y\,j$ and $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}.$"] ["question-8399ab15-70cf-5db8-b1d1-61088de736be" :question/worked-solution "We will use the fact that

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r.
$$

We're given the value of the first integral, so we only need to work out the second.

The path ${C}_{2}$ is the section of the curve $y=-{x}^{3}$ from $A$ to $O.$ It can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}(t)=t\,i-{t}^{3}\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $-2\le t\le 0.$ Along this curve, we have $x=t$ and $y=-{t}^{3}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{2}(t)) & =xy\,i+y\,j \\  & =-{t}^{4}\,i-{t}^{3}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivative, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-{t}^{3})j \\  & =i-3{t}^{2}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

We can now compute the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{2}(t))\cdot {r}_{2}^{′}(t) & =(-{t}^{4}\,i-{t}^{3}\,j)\cdot (i-3{t}^{2}\,j) \\  & =-{t}^{4}+3{t}^{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =16+{\int }_{-2}^{0}F({r}_{2}(t))\cdot {r}_{2}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =16+{\int }_{-2}^{0}(-{t}^{4}+3{t}^{5})\,\text{d}t \\  & =16+{[-\frac{1}{5}{t}^{5}+\frac{1}{2}{t}^{6}]}_{-2}^{0} \\  & =16+[0-(-\frac{(-{2}^{5})}{5}+\frac{(-2)^{6}}{2})] \\  & =16-\frac{192}{5} \\  & =-\frac{112}{5}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-8399ab15-70cf-5db8-b1d1-61088de736be" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-b523b1e1-5cbd-5efb-b1af-a137b9b5cd25" :answer-field/id #uuid Given that $\displaystyle \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = -4,$ evaluate $\displaystyle \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r},$ where $\mathbf{F}(x, y) = (2x-3y) \,\mathbf{i} + (2y-5x)\,\mathbf {j}$ and $C = C_1\cup C_2.$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the fact that

$$
\int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r}
+
 \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r}.
$$

We're given the value of the first integral, so we only need to work out the second.

The path $C_2$ is the line segment from $O$ to $B.$ It can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}(t) & =b+t(c-b) \\  & =⟨0,0⟩+t(⟨1,1⟩-⟨0,0⟩) \\  & =⟨t,t⟩ \\  & =t\,i+t\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0 \lt t \lt 1.$ Along this segment, we have $x = t$ and $y = t.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{2}(t)) & =(2x-3y)\,i+(2y-5x)\,j \\  & =(2t-3t)\,i+(2t-5t)\,j \\  & =-t\,i-3t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivative, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =i+j\end{aligned}
$$

We can now compute the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{2}(t))\cdot {r}_{2}^{′}(t) & =(-t\,i-3t\,j)\cdot (i+j) \\  & =-t\cdot 1+(-3t)\cdot 1 \\  & =-4t\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =-4+{\int }_{0}^{1}F({r}_{2}(t))\cdot {r}_{2}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-4+{\int }_{0}^{1}(-4t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-4+[-2{t}^{2}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =-4+[-2+0] \\  & =-6\end{aligned}

We list two of them below:

- If $-C$ denotes the path obtained by reversing the orientation of $C,$ then

$$
\int\limits_{-C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r = -\int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r.
$$

- If $C = C_1\cup C_2$ is the union of two paths $C_1$ and $C_2$, then

$$
\int\limits_{C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r 
= 
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r + \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r.
$$

The first property has an intuitive meaning if we think about it in terms of the work done by a force on a particle. To see this, consider the vector field $\mathbf F$ and the line segment $\overline{AB},$ shown below. Let $C$ be the path defined by traversing the line segment from $A$ to $B.$

![](images/4f/4f69f80d98d301410908f7ec867a89bdc834c22a51f224d9b00b80ceca39ab87.png)

Let $W(C)$ be the work done in moving the particle along $C.$ Since our particle moves in the same direction as the vector field, we have

$$
W(C) = \int\limits_{C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r > 0.
$$

However, if we move the particle from $B$ to $A,$ we expect the line integral to be negative. This is because the particle is now moving against $\mathbf F.$ 

![](images/fe/fe6b2e67d33a4993104406c88b1dc0dc897be33d034007ed581a75f741ddf620.png)

Therefore,

$$
W(-C) = \int\limits_{-C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r < 0.
$$

We can show that the work done in moving the particle along $-C$ is the same as the work done in moving it along $C$ but with the opposite sign. That is

$$
W(-C) = -W(C).
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\int\limits_{-C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r = -\int\limits_{C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "d745eed3-7e69-55af-b685-1c7482dfffb9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3976 :tutorial/title "Reversing the Orientation of a Curve and Sums Over Unions of Paths"} :step/id #uuid $$
\mathbf F(x,y) = P(x,y)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y)\,\mathbf j
$$

$$
\mathbf r (t) = x(t)\,\mathbf i + y(t)\,\mathbf j, \qquad t\in [a,b].
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{'}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}(P(x(t),y(t))\,i+Q(x(t),y(t))\,j)\cdot (\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j)\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}(P(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+Q(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}P(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+Q(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{C}P(x,y)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F\cdot\textrm d \mathbf r  = \int\limits_C P(x,y)\,\textrm d x + Q(x,y)  \,\textrm d y
$$

Consider a vector field $\mathbf F$ on $\mathbb R^2$ with components $P$ and $Q\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\mathbf F(x,y) = P(x,y)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y)\,\mathbf j
$$

Now suppose that $C$ is a smooth curve on $\mathbb R^2,$ given by

$$
\mathbf r (t) = x(t)\,\mathbf i + y(t)\,\mathbf j, \qquad t\in [a,b].
$$

Then, we can write the line integral of $\mathbf F$ along $C$ as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{'}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}(P(x(t),y(t))\,i+Q(x(t),y(t))\,j)\cdot (\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j)\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}(P(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+Q(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}P(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+Q(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{C}P(x,y)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following formula:

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F\cdot\textrm d \mathbf r  = \int\limits_C P(x,y)\,\textrm d x + Q(x,y)  \,\textrm d y
$$

An analogous result holds for vector fields on $\mathbb R^3.$ That is, 

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F\cdot\textrm d \mathbf r  = \int\limits_C P(x,y,z)\,\textrm d x + Q(x,y,z)  \,\textrm d y + R(x,y,z) \,\textrm d z
$$

where $\mathbf F(x,y,z) = P(x,y,z)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y,z)\,\mathbf j + R(x,y,z)\,\mathbf k.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b4ca8cae-81df-5c55-90ac-839b063e78a6" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5837 :tutorial/title
